title: CI/CD
description: Secrets, environments, and scaling pipelines across many repositories and combinations.
resumo: Secrets in GitHub Secrets or OIDC, passed as env vars to the step that needs them, never printed.
Build once, promote the same image to every environment.
Reusable workflows (`workflow_call`) for one standard pipeline — pinned to a version, never `@main`.
Matrix builds test combinations in parallel; add a summary job to require in branch protection.
Feature flags separate deploy from release — and must be removed after the rollout.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** the pipeline needs a registry password, a Sonar token and cloud credentials. Written in the YAML, they end up in Git and in the logs.

**Concept:** credentials live in GitHub Secrets (per repository or per environment) and are read as `${{ secrets.NAME }}`; GitHub masks their values in the logs. Give the `GITHUB_TOKEN` only the permissions each job needs with `permissions`. For the cloud, prefer OIDC: the workflow exchanges a short-lived token for temporary credentials, with no long-lived keys stored anywhere.

**How it works:** pass secrets as environment variables to the step that needs them, and nowhere else.
examples.code:
permissions:
  contents: read
  id-token: write   # required for OIDC

steps:
  - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
    with:
      role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/deploy-api
      aws-region: us-east-1
  - name: Sonar analysis
    env:
      SONAR_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.SONAR_TOKEN }}
    run: ./mvnw -B sonar:sonar
examples.interview_question: How do you use credentials in a pipeline without exposing them?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Printing a secret, trusting the masking. GitHub masks the exact value, but a transformed value — Base64, split, URL-encoded — is printed in clear. Never print secrets.
examples.code:
# WRONG
- run: echo "${{ secrets.SONAR_TOKEN }}" | base64     # the encoded value is NOT masked

# RIGHT: hand it to the tool as an environment variable, never print it
- env:
    SONAR_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.SONAR_TOKEN }}
  run: ./mvnw -B sonar:sonar

subsections.subtitle: Environments and Promotion
subsections.description: Dev, staging and production with the same artifact.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** it worked in staging and broke in production — and production was built from a different compilation.

**Concept:** rebuilding for each environment can produce different binaries (updated dependencies, another compiler), which invalidates the tests done in staging. Build once and promote the same image, changing only the configuration (environment variables, profiles). GitHub Environments add protection rules, such as required reviewers before production.

**How it works:** the production job deploys the image tagged with the same commit SHA that passed staging.
examples.code:
deploy-production:
  needs: deploy-staging
  runs-on: ubuntu-latest
  environment:
    name: production              # requires approval, configured in the repository
    url: https://api.shop.com
  steps:
    - run: ./deploy.sh ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:${{ github.sha }}
examples.interview_question: Why promote the same artifact between environments instead of rebuilding?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: A separate build per environment. The image in production was never tested; what passed staging was a different binary.
examples.code:
# WRONG
deploy-staging:     ./mvnw package && docker build -t api:staging .
deploy-production:  ./mvnw package && docker build -t api:prod .

# RIGHT: one build, the same tag everywhere
build:              docker build -t api:${{ github.sha }} .
deploy-staging:     deploy api:${{ github.sha }}
deploy-production:  deploy api:${{ github.sha }}

subsections.subtitle: Reusable Pipelines
subsections.description: One standard pipeline for many repositories.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** thirty services each have their own copy of the pipeline; a security fix means thirty pull requests, and half of them drift.

**Concept:** in GitHub Actions, reusable workflows (`workflow_call`) let a central repository define the standard pipeline — Maven build, tests, image, scan — and each service just calls it with parameters. Composite actions bundle sequences of steps. An improvement then reaches every service at once, with the version pinned by tag.

**How it works:** services pin a version (`@v3`) and upgrade deliberately; the central repository follows semantic versioning.
examples.code:
# Central repository: .github/workflows/java-service.yml
on:
  workflow_call:
    inputs:
      java-version: { type: string, default: '21' }

# In each service: .github/workflows/ci.yml
jobs:
  pipeline:
    uses: shop/pipelines/.github/workflows/java-service.yml@v3
    with:
      java-version: '21'
    secrets: inherit
examples.interview_question: How do you avoid duplicating the same pipeline across dozens of repositories?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Calling the shared workflow from `@main`. Every change in the central repository instantly reaches every service — one mistake breaks thirty pipelines at once. Pin a released version.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** a library must work on Java 17 and 21, on Linux and Windows, and testing each combination one after the other takes an hour.

**Concept:** a matrix runs the same job for every combination of parameters — JDK versions, operating systems, databases — in parallel. It is useful for libraries that support several versions, or to split a big test suite into shards. `fail-fast` cancels the other combinations when one fails.

**How it works:** keep the matrix to the combinations you really support; each one costs runner minutes.
examples.code:
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    strategy:
      fail-fast: true
      matrix:
        os: [ubuntu-latest, windows-latest]
        java: ['17', '21']
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-java@v4
        with:
          distribution: temurin
          java-version: ${{ matrix.java }}
          cache: maven
      - run: ./mvnw -B verify
examples.interview_question: What is a matrix strategy for?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Requiring the matrix job by its plain name in branch protection. Each combination is reported as a separate check (`test (ubuntu-latest, 17)`), so the required "test" check never appears and the PR waits forever — or nothing is required at all. Require each combination, or add one summary job that `needs` the matrix.
examples.code:
# RIGHT: one stable check to require in branch protection
  all-tests:
    needs: test
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    if: always()
    steps:
      - run: test "${{ needs.test.result }}" = "success"

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** an unfinished feature blocks the merge for weeks, and when it finally goes out there is no quick way to turn it off.

**Concept:** a feature flag decides at runtime whether a feature is on. The code goes to production switched off (deploy) and is turned on later, for everyone or for a percentage of users (release). That enables trunk-based development, A/B tests, and kill switches that disable a broken feature without a new deploy.

**How it works:** remove a flag once the feature is fully released; every flag left behind is a branch in the code to maintain and test.
examples.interview_question: How do feature flags let you deploy unfinished code safely?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Flags that are never removed. A year later the code has dozens of `if (flag)` branches, nobody knows which combinations are tested, and turning an old flag off breaks something.
